extracted.intended_audience: patent owners and patent practitioners (in-house and outside counsel) advising clients on options after AIA post-grant claim cancellations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent owners and counsel on available remedies and strategic considerations after claims are cancelled in AIA post-grant proceedings (IPR, PGR, CBM), including procedural standards, timing, benefits, risks, and likely outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter Partes Review (IPR) institution and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR is a trial proceeding to challenge patentability of one or more claims under 35 U.S.C. § 102 and/or § 103 based only on patents or printed publications; almost any party except the patentee may file; timing: available after the later of nine months after patent issuance or after any pending PGR has ended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A three-judge APJ panel determines whether there is a 'reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 claim challenged in the petition' (35 U.S.C. § 314(a)). If instituted, PTAB issues a final determination within one year (extendable for good cause by six months). Statutory estoppel: if a final decision is reached, the petitioner is estopped in district court/ITC from raising any ground it 'raised or reasonably could have raised' in the IPR, and the patent owner is estopped from prosecuting patentably indistinct claims (35 U.S.C. § 315(e); 37 C.F.R. § 42.73). Use these timing and estoppel rules when assessing whether to file or defend an IPR and when planning parallel district/ITC litigation or further prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covered Business Method (CBM) review requirements and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: CBM review is a PTAB trial to review patentability of claims in a 'covered business method' patent (claims to a method or apparatus related to a financial product or service, not a technological invention). Only a person accused of infringement may file a CBM petition; CBM can be filed before litigation or after complaint service, subject to other timing limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institution standard: 'more likely than not' that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable (35 U.S.C. § 324). CBM may be based on any ground of invalidity (§§ 101, 102, 103, 112). CBM is a transitional program (sunset on Sept. 16, 2020). If a final decision issues, the petitioner is estopped from raising in litigation any ground 'raised' in the CBM, and from raising in subsequent PTO proceedings any ground that 'reasonably could have been raised' in CBM; patent owner estopped from prosecuting patentably indistinct claims (AIA § 18; 37 C.F.R. § 42.73). These constraints affect whether to pursue CBM and how to structure litigation and prosecution strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Grant Review (PGR) institution and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: PGR is a PTAB trial to review patentability of claims under a broad set of grounds (35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 102, 103, 112) for patents issuing from first-inventor-to-file applications; a non-owner who has not previously filed a civil action challenging validity may file on or prior to nine months after issuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institution standard: 'more likely than not' that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable (35 U.S.C. § 321(b)). If instituted and not dismissed, PTAB issues a final determination within one year (extendable by six months). After institution, the petitioner is precluded from re-litigating in a civil action any issue it raised or reasonably could have raised in the PGR. Use the broader grounds and early filing window (within nine months) when evaluating the advisability and timing of a PGR petition vs. IPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to amend during post-grant proceedings (statutory limit and constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: During IPR, CBM or PGR, the patent owner may file one motion to amend the patent (35 U.S.C. § 316(d)); substitute claims may not 'enlarge the scope' of the claims or 'introduce new subject matter' (37 C.F.R. § 42.121(a)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests to cancel claims are typically granted without substantive review; substitute-claim motions are generally decided only when the panel first determines the original claims are unpatentable (many motions are contingent on an unfavorable decision for original claims). The PTAB's Motion to Amend study (Apr. 30, 2016) shows motions to amend were decided on the merits in a small fraction of trials (118/1539, 8%), and of those decided on the merits only 5% were granted-in-part/ granted. Denial reasons included: anticipation/obviousness over art of record (35%), multiple statutory reasons (23%), lack of written description (8%), non-statutory subject matter (6%), claim enlargement (5%), unreasonable number of substitute claims (3%), indefiniteness (1%), and procedural failures such as failure to show substitute claims are patentable over 'the prior art in general' (19%). These high denial rates and common denial rationales should guide patent owners' decision whether to attempt amendment in PTAB proceedings vs. pursue other remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aqua Products en banc questions (burden allocation and Board authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending en banc Federal Circuit questions regarding motions to amend focus on whether the PTO may require patent owners to bear the burden of persuasion or production on patentability of amended claims and whether the Board may sua sponte raise patentability challenges to proposed amended claims when the petitioner does not challenge them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolution of these questions will clarify standards for motions to amend in IPRs and could materially affect how difficult it is for patent owners to obtain substitute claims. Consider that current practice and Board authority on burdens and sua sponte actions may affect motion strategy and the likelihood of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing request standard and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: After a final PTAB decision, a patent owner may file a request for rehearing within 30 days of entry of the final written decision (37 C.F.R. § 42.71(d)). The request 'must specifically identify all matters the party believes the Board misapprehended or overlooked, and the place where each matter was previously addressed in a motion, an opposition, or a reply.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A panel reviews a rehearing request for abuse of discretion (37 C.F.R. § 42.71(c)). The PTAB rarely grants rehearing of final written decisions. Consider whether clear error exists before filing; advantage: PTAB must further explain its rationale and that explanation could aid an appeal; disadvantage: PTAB may bolster its rationale prior to appeal, possibly making reversal harder. Use precise, pointed argumentation and cite where matters were previously raised when drafting a rehearing petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (timing and standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may appeal a final written PTAB decision by filing a notice of appeal within 63 days after the final written decision or rehearing decision (35 U.S.C. §§ 319, 329). On appeal, legal conclusions are reviewed de novo and factual findings under the substantial evidence standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals are a case-by-case decision balancing costs/time and likely success. Historical data through Apr. 24, 2016 indicate the Federal Circuit affirmed the majority of PTAB decisions on appeal (83% affirmed in a set of 77 decisions from 110 IPR petitions; 10% affirmed-in-part/ reversed-in-part or vacated-in-part; 7% reversed/vacated/remanded). The Federal Circuit may not reweigh evidence and will sustain PTAB findings if they articulat[e] 'logical and rational' reasons. Patent owners should assess whether appeal can show PTAB failed to articulate an adequate rationale or misapplied law, and weigh the relatively low reversal rate when deciding to appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue application (statutory basis, scope, benefits, and risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue application under 35 U.S.C. § 251 may be filed when a patent is 'through error, deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid' due to defective specification/drawing or claiming more/less than the patentee had a right to claim. Reissue can be used to pursue amended (often narrower) claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: patent owner may prosecute narrower claims to avoid estoppel and to present different arguments over prior art; may pursue broader claims if filed within two years of issuance (broadening reissue), and may file continuing reissue applications claiming priority to the first reissue. Risks: reissue requires surrender of the original patent and reopens prosecution — examiner may reject claims on new grounds; doctrine of intervening rights may limit damages for amended claims to the period after issuance of the reissued claim; third parties may file protests or later challenge the reissue via PGR, IPR, or CBM. Pendency: average reissue pendency decreased to ~2.3 years for reissued patents through Apr. 2016 (previously ~5 years). Weigh pendency, possible reexamination, intervening rights, and the possibility of additional challenges when choosing reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental examination (35 U.S.C. § 257) and triggering ex parte reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may request supplemental examination to 'consider, reconsider, or correct information believed to be relevant to the patent' (35 U.S.C. § 257). The request must include a detailed explanation of the relevance and manner of applying each item of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO director determines within three months whether the information raises a substantial new question of patentability (SNQP); if so, ex parte reexamination is instituted, and ex parte reexamination is not limited to patents/printed publications. Benefit: if supplemental examination and any resulting ex parte reexamination are completed before certain civil actions or ITC proceedings, a court or the PTO cannot hold the patent unenforceable based on conduct regarding information considered during supplemental examination (35 U.S.C. § 257(c)(1)), subject to exceptions (e.g., prior allegations in civil actions or FDCA notices). Items submitted may include information beyond patents/printed publications, which can be an advantage over ex parte reexamination alone. Use supplemental examination to attempt to immunize the patent from inequitable conduct defenses, but be mindful of the timing constraints and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte reexamination (grounds, process, and tradeoffs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex parte reexamination may be instituted based on a substantial new question of patentability shown by patents and printed publications (and double patenting in some contexts), and it is an ex parte proceeding between the patent owner and the PTO examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages vs. PTAB motions: generally involves only the patent owner and PTO; may allow full examination (interviews, RCEs, appeals to the PTAB), claim amendments without admitting an error (unlike reissue), and can be potentially quicker than a reissue. Disadvantages: reexamination may result in invalidation on additional grounds (patents are not presumed valid in reexamination contexts as in district court), may trigger intervening rights if claims are substantively amended, and pendency can still be lengthy (historical averages around 1.8–2.3 years in recent years). Consider ex parte reexamination when seeking amendment without surrendering the original patent and when controlling public exposure to third-party submissions is desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation application strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecuting a continuation application that claims priority to the parent patent can be used to pursue patentably distinct claims if a continuation application remains pending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During continuation prosecution the patent owner can account for arguments and prior art raised in the post-grant proceeding to draft claims that are patentably distinct from cancelled claims. Consider the costs and time of prosecution versus the likelihood of obtaining useful claims; continuations require a pending application that can be amended/prosecuted and can be a preferred route when reissue or reexamination present unacceptable risks or pendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel effects from AIA post-grant proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: If a post-grant proceeding reaches a final written decision, estoppel provisions restrict parties' future ability to litigate or prosecute certain invalidity grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR/CBM/PGR estoppel rules: petitioners are estopped in district court or ITC from raising any invalidity ground they 'raised or reasonably could have raised' in the post-grant proceeding (35 U.S.C. § 315(e) and related provisions); petitioners in CBM are similarly estopped from raising grounds 'raised' in CBM, and from raising in subsequent PTO proceedings any ground that 'reasonably could have been raised' in CBM; patent owners are estopped from prosecuting claims that are patentably indistinct from invalidated claims (37 C.F.R. § 42.73; AIA provisions). These estoppel consequences should be a central consideration when choosing between defending at the PTAB, appealing, or pursuing prosecution-based remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution standards and timing comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Different AIA proceedings apply different institution standards and timing rules and have similar one-year final-decision clocks (extendable six months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR institution standard: 'reasonable likelihood' petitioner would prevail on at least one claim (35 U.S.C. § 314(a)). CBM and PGR institution standard: 'more likely than not' that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable (35 U.S.C. §§ 321(b), 324). IPRs are available after the later of nine months post-issuance or after conclusion of any PGR; PGR must be filed within nine months of issuance for eligible patents. Final PTAB determinations are expected within one year of institution (extendable by six months for good cause). CBM is a transitional program with a sunset date (Sept. 16, 2020). Use these institution standards and timing windows when choosing the most appropriate challenge or defense strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical statistics on post-grant proceedings and motions to amend (empirical context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical PTAB/PTO statistics show high rates of claim cancellation in completed post-grant proceedings and low success rates for motions to amend decided on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of Sept. 30, 2016: 5,656 petitions filed (91% IPR, 8% CBM, 1% PGR). Of IPR petitions completed to date, 1,214 reached final written decisions and 85% cancelled all or some claims. Of CBM petitions completed to date, 143 reached final written decisions and 98% cancelled all or some claims. PTAB Motion to Amend Study (Apr. 30, 2016) reported the Board decided merits of substitute-claim motions in only 118 of 1539 completed AIA trials (8%); of those 118, motions were granted or granted-in-part in 6 trials (5%) and denied in 112 (95%). Reasons for denial (with percentages) are summarized in the MTA study (anticipation/obviousness 35%; multiple statutory reasons 23%; lack of written description 8%; non-statutory subject matter 6%; etc.). These data should inform realistic expectations about likelihood of preserving original claim scope or obtaining substitute claims via PTAB proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative benefits and risks table for post-decision options
rubrics_metrics.description: High-level comparison of standards, benefits, and risks for rehearing, appeal, reissue, supplemental examination, ex parte reexamination, and continuation applications, to guide option selection after claims are cancelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rehearing: must identify misapprehensions, reviewed for abuse of discretion; advantage: may elicit additional rationale useful on appeal; risk: rarely granted and may bolster PTAB rationale. Appeal to Federal Circuit: de novo review of legal questions, substantial evidence for facts; advantage: potential reversal but historically low reversal rates; cost/time considerations. Reissue: full prosecution, can seek broader claims within two years (but surrender original patent); advantage: full examination and potential for broadened or alternative claims; risks: intervening rights, reopened prosecution, third-party protests, pendency. Supplemental examination: can immunize against unenforceability (if completed before certain litigation), broader submission scope than ex parte reexam; risk: exceptions if prior allegations exist. Ex parte reexamination: ex parte process with examiner, possibly quicker than reissue, may allow amendments without admitting error; risk: patents not presumed valid, intervening rights if claims amended. Continuation: maintain pending application to pursue patentably distinct claims informed by PTAB record; cost/time tradeoffs. Use the summarized benefits/risks to select one or more options to preserve rights post-cancellation, frequently combining strategies (e.g., appeal plus reissue or continuation) based on business objectives and timelines.
